passages.t: ‘His loving devotion endures forever’: the refrain, 26 times
passages.happening:
Psalm 136 has one line that comes back in every verse. “Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good. His loving devotion endures forever” (verse 1). “Give thanks to the God of gods. His loving devotion endures forever” (verse 2). “Give thanks to the Lord of lords” (verse 3).

The second half of each verse is always the same. In the BSB, ‘His loving devotion endures forever’ comes 26 times, once in each of its 26 verses.

The first half of each verse tells what God has done. First comes creation. “He alone does great wonders” (verse 4). “By His insight He made the heavens” (verse 5). He spread out the earth (verse 6). He made the great lights, “the sun to rule the day” and “the moon and stars to govern the night” (verses 8 and 9). After every one comes the answer: his loving devotion endures forever.
passages.hearers:
Picture a leader, perhaps one of the Levite singers, calling out the first half of each line, and the whole crowd shouting back the second. Even a child, or someone who could not read, could join in. Ezra tells of such singing when the foundation of the second temple was laid: “they sang responsively” (Ezra 3:11). The same refrain was sung when David brought the ark to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:34) and when Solomon's temple was filled with the cloud (2 Chronicles 5:13).

‘Loving devotion’ is the Hebrew word hesed. The book page explains it: God's loyal love, kept because he bound himself by promise. It comes 26 times in this psalm alone.

‘God of gods’ and ‘Lord of lords’ are the language of a world full of gods and kings. Great kings called themselves ‘king of kings’. The psalm does not stop to argue. It simply says the LORD is above every power anyone could name.

In the Talmud this psalm is called the Great Hallel, ‘the great praise’. One teacher there links the name to verse 25, where God gives food to every creature. Jewish families say it at the Passover meal to this day, after the Hallel of Psalms 113 to 118.
passages.later:
Lamentations, written in grief over Jerusalem, holds on to the same truth: “Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail. They are new every morning” (Lamentations 3:22-23).

Paul was sure that nothing “will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:39).
passages.asks:
Try reading Psalm 136 aloud with someone else, one of you reading the first half of each verse and the other answering. You will feel why it was written this way.

The refrain is the answer to every line, whether the line is about the stars or about a hard day in Egypt. What would it be like to answer each part of your own story with ‘His loving devotion endures forever’?

passages.t: From Egypt to ‘He remembered us in our low estate’
passages.happening:
Now the psalm tells Israel's story, still with the refrain after every line. God struck down Egypt's firstborn and “brought Israel out from among them” (verses 10 and 11), “with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm” (verse 12). “He divided the Red Sea in two” (verse 13), led Israel through, and swept Pharaoh's army into the sea (verses 14 and 15). “He led His people through the wilderness” (verse 16).

He struck down great kings, Sihon and Og (verses 17 to 20), and gave their land to Israel (verses 21 and 22).

Then the story comes closer. “He remembered us in our low estate” (verse 23) “and freed us from our enemies” (verse 24). Then it opens out to the whole world. “He gives food to every creature” (verse 25). It ends where it began. “Give thanks to the God of heaven! His loving devotion endures forever” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
‘A mighty hand and an outstretched arm’ is the way Deuteronomy speaks of the exodus, again and again. A first hearer would know it at once.

Notice the move in verse 23. The psalm has been telling of long-ago events. Now it says ‘us’. The people singing it, perhaps after the exile, put themselves in the story. Their ‘low estate’ may be the exile itself. The God who brought their ancestors out of Egypt has remembered them too.

Verse 25 widens the circle again. God's loving devotion is not only for Israel. He feeds every living thing.

Sihon and Og were kings who came out to fight Israel when Israel asked to pass through their land (Numbers 21:23-24).
passages.later: Mary sang that God “has looked with favor on the humble state of His servant” (Luke 1:48), words close to verse 23. Jesus pointed to the birds: “your heavenly Father feeds them” (Matthew 6:26), as verse 25 says.
passages.hard: How can a psalm sing of God's love right after the death of Egypt's firstborn and the defeat of kings? The psalm tells the story as it was felt by slaves set free: for them, the end of Pharaoh's power was what God's love looked like. Scripture also says God takes no pleasure in anyone's death: “Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked? declares the Lord GOD” (Ezekiel 18:23). Christians hold these together in different ways, and the note on Psalm 106 sets out how they read the conquest stories. No reading of these verses gives anyone today a right to harm another person or people.
passages.asks:
Where has God remembered you ‘in your low estate’? The psalm moves from the great events of history to ‘us’. It invites you to do the same: to see your own life inside God's long story of loving devotion.

And verse 25 asks you to notice the ordinary. Every meal is a line in this psalm.
